patch.objective: Explain stability using the center of gravity, the base of support and whether the line of gravity falls within it
secondaryObjectives: Explain how the baroreceptor reflex keeps blood pressure up on standing, and how the skeletal muscle pump and venous valves return blood to the heart

sources.cite: OpenStax, College Physics for AP Courses, 9.3 Stability
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch: 'The critical point is reached when the cg is no longer above the base of support'; spreading the feet gives 'a larger base of support', so the center of gravity can shift further before it leaves the base. The PTPREREQ course cites OpenStax College Physics for this unit. The case: a man four months after a stroke who falls getting up at night; a gait belt and guarding when he is up, and a seat at once when he is light-headed, because a body whose center of gravity leaves its base falls.

sources.cite: Physical Therapy Management of Fall Risk in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: An Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline From the American Physical Therapy Association. J Geriatr Phys Ther. 2025;48. doi:10.1519/JPT.0000000000000454 (PMC12533762)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11 in the Europe PMC full text. Fall risk: Berg below 50, TUG over 11 s, five times sit-to-stand over 12 s, single-leg stance under 6.5 s, self-selected gait speed under 1.0 m/s. Exercise must be at least 150 minutes to 3 hours a week for 6 to 12 months and include progressive, sufficiently challenging balance training (level I, strong).

sources.cite: Moore JL, Potter K, Blankshain K, et al. A core set of outcome measures for adults with neurologic conditions undergoing rehabilitation: a clinical practice guideline. J Neurol Phys Ther. 2018;42:174-220. doi:10.1097/NPT.0000000000000229 (PMC6023606)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11 in the Europe PMC full text. The core set: Berg Balance Scale, Activities-specific Balance Confidence Scale, Functional Gait Assessment, 10 meter Walk Test, 6-Minute Walk Test, and the 5 Times Sit-to-Stand (best practice). APTA lists it as current with an update in progress.

sources.cite: Hornby TG, Reisman DS, Ward IG, et al. Clinical practice guideline to improve locomotor function following chronic stroke, incomplete spinal cord injury, and brain injury. J Neurol Phys Ther. 2020;44(1):49-100. doi:10.1097/NPT.0000000000000303
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11 in a repository copy of the published article. Action statement 1: use moderate- to high-intensity walking training (60-80% of heart rate reserve or up to 85% of maximum heart rate) for chronic stroke (strong); record HR and RPE at regular intervals; consult the physician before higher-intensity training. Action statement 6A: do not perform sitting or standing balance training aimed at postural stability to improve walking speed or distance.

sources.cite: APTA Acute Care and APTA Cardiovascular and Pulmonary, Adult Vital Sign Interpretation in Acute Care Guide 2021 (boards approved March and April 2021)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11 through a text extraction of the PDF. Normal exercise response: HR rises about 10 beats/min per MET and returns to the pre-exercise level in 3-5 min; SBP rises about 10 mmHg per MET. Stop criteria include SBP drop >10 mmHg with increasing workload, new or worsening dysrhythmia, RR >40, unable to speak comfortably, SpO2 <90% or a drop of 4% or more (acute coronary syndrome), SpO2 <85% (lung disease); lung disease activity target 88-92%. Orthostatic hypotension: SBP drop >20 or DBP drop >10 mmHg within 3 min of standing. Beta blockers: lower HR with exercise and a dampened BP response; use the RPE scale in addition to HR.

sources.cite: American Society of Nuclear Cardiology, Practice Points: Exercise Stress Testing (Weinberg R, Bullock-Palmer R)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11. Indications for early termination of exercise include a hypertensive response (systolic BP over 250 mmHg and/or diastolic over 115 mmHg). The document is undated; the URL path is dated May 2024.
